title: Nullable value semantics — in-band sentinels + null-fallback arithmetic
body:
## What it is

A value can be present or absent. An absent value is `null`. Doing arithmetic with a `null` simply produces `null` again instead of stopping your program.

Null costs no space, because each type spends one of its own values on it — an **in-band sentinel**:

| type | the value that means null |
|---|---|
| `integer` | the most negative 64-bit integer |
| `float` / `single` | NaN |
| `boolean` | `false` |
| `character` | the NUL character (code point 0) |
| `text` | a single NUL character — the empty string `""` is NOT null |
| a reference | record 0 |
| a plain `enum` | byte 255 (which is why an enum stops at 255 variants) |

So a value that happens to BE the sentinel reads as absent. `false` is the one to know: for a boolean, "not set" and "set to false" are the same value, and no check can separate them.

## How it aids you

Missing data — a lookup that found nothing, a field never filled in — no longer has to be a special case that crashes. The absence flows through your calculation as `null`, so you can carry on and decide what to do about it at the end rather than guarding every step. Nothing is boxed and nothing is wrapped, so an optional value costs exactly what the value costs.

The price is that null is a value of the type, not a separate thing beside it. For a `boolean` that bites at once, since its null IS `false`; for an `integer` the reserved value is one real arithmetic almost never reaches. The same shape then repeats one level up, in any API that answers a legitimate value to mean "nothing here" — and there the collision is ordinary rather than rare, so the bound has to come from somewhere else.

## Example

```loft
fn main() {
    a = null as integer?;  // a holds no value
    b = a + 10;            // arithmetic on null gives null, no crash
    println("{a} {b}");    // null null
    println("still running");
}
```

## In real use

Where this feature carries real work, validated by `check_doc_drift.sh examples`:

Example: @GFX-003 — `get_pixel` answers 0 off the canvas, and 0 is a colour the canvas holds, so the answer cannot tell "outside" from "transparent black"
Example: @TIM-002 — what a library's null MEANS is the library's to say: `parse` answers null for text that is not shaped like a date, never for a date that is not real

title: `??` null-coalescing operator (incl. `?? return`)
body:
## What it is

The `??` operator supplies a fallback: `value ?? fallback` gives you `value` when it has one, and `fallback` when `value` is null.

## How it aids you

It turns "this might be missing" into "here is a sensible default" in a single, readable step — no `if`-checks around every optional value. You state the backup once, right where the value is used.

A fallback is a decision, not a repair. `??` fires only on a **null**, so it cannot see a value that is present and wrong — a float divided by zero is an infinity, not a null (@F38), and `x / d ?? 0.0` hands that infinity straight on. Where the failure is not a null, guard the input instead.

## Example

```loft
fn main() {
    missing = null as integer?;
    count = missing ?? 0;       // use 0 when the value is null
    name = "Ada" ?? "unknown";  // keeps the real value when present
    println("{count} {name}");  // 0 Ada
}
```

## In real use

Where this feature carries real work, validated by `check_doc_drift.sh examples`:

Example: @MSH-005 — `normalize3` divides by a length and discharges with `?? 0.0`, so a degenerate camera answers a zero matrix rather than an error
Example: @FTR-005 — which arithmetic failures `??` can reach, and which it cannot

title: Primitive scalar types (integer, float, single, boolean, character)
Ranged/width integer types (u8/i8/u16/i16/i32/u32)
body:
## What it is

Besides the everyday `integer`, loft offers smaller number types sized to their range: `u8`, `i8`, `u16`, `i16`, `i32`, `u32`. Each holds whole numbers within fixed bounds and takes up less space.

## How it aids you

When you store many numbers you know stay small — a colour channel (0..255), an age, a year — these compact types keep your data small and your intent clear, while you still write and read them like ordinary numbers.

## Example

```loft
fn main() {
    level: u8 = 200;      // fits in a single byte (0..255)
    year: u16 = 2026;     // fits in two bytes
    temp: i8 = -40;       // small signed value
    println("{level} {year} {temp}");   // 200 2026 -40
}
```


## Where the bounds are enforced — one answer, in every position

Every position now bounds the value the same way, and a result that does not fit takes the
type's **default** — never a wrapped or truncated one, which would be in range,
type-correct and unrelated to the calculation (`formal/operational.md` `(E-Uncomp-NN)`).

| position | out-of-range | result |
|---|---|---|
| declaration — `l: u8 = 300` | | refused: *"cannot implicitly narrow integer to u8"* |
| written-out assignment — `l = l + 10` | | refused, same message |
| compound assignment — `l: u8 = 250; l += 10` | 260 | `0` |
| `b: u8 = 5; b -= 10` | -5 | `0` |
| struct field — `u.a += 253` from 7 | 260 | `0` |
| vector element — `v[0] += 253` from 7 | 260 | `0` |

`i32` is the one exception, and it is a representation fact rather than a rule change: it
keeps `i32::MIN` back for null, so its overflow reads as `null` where the other five, which
use every code they have, read as the default.

## Choosing the value, and seeing that it did not fit

Because the five that fill their range have no code left for a failure, `0` from an overflow
and a computed `0` are the same value. Two spellings — both ordinary, neither new — let an
author who cares about that edge handle it:

```loft
n: integer = 400;
level: u8 = n ?? 255;        // 255 — YOUR value instead of the type's default

health: u8 = 250;
health += 10;
if !health { … }             // true: the store did not fit (health is 0, as it would be anyway)
```

The `if` has to be the **very next** statement after the store — further away there would be
nowhere to keep the answer but the number itself, which would cost a `vector<u8>` the byte
the type was chosen for. Move it and the compiler tells you the check stopped working rather
than letting it go quiet.

The storage half of the promise holds exactly: `u8` is 1 byte, `u16` 2, `i32`/`u32` 4,
against `integer`'s 8, and a struct is their packed sum — `{ a: u8, b: u16, c: i8 }` is 4. A
`vector<u8>` of three elements is three bytes.

## In real use

Example: @FTR-043 — a width type's bounds: enforced at the declaration and in storage, absent on a local reached by `+=`

title: Type conversions — implicit, format-only, and explicit `as`
body:
## What it is

The `as` cast converts a value from one type to another on purpose: `pi as integer`, `"42" as integer?`, `'A' as integer`. You ask for the conversion, so it happens exactly where you write it.

## How it aids you

You get to move between types deliberately — round a decimal down to a whole number, read a number out of text, get a character's code — with the conversion visible in the code. Nothing silently changes type behind your back.

Whether a cast can REFUSE is the target type's choice, not the cast's. `"42" as integer?` has a null channel and answers null on rubbish; a cast to a type with no null — a `value struct` (@F95) — cannot, so it is total and bad input arrives as an ordinary-looking value of that type. Read the target's own documentation before treating a cast as a check.

## Example

```loft
fn main() {
    pi: float = 3.75;
    whole = pi as integer;      // 3  (drops the fraction)
    parsed = "42" as integer?;  // text turned into a number (or null)
    code = 'A' as integer;      // 65 (the character's code)
    println("{whole} {parsed} {code}");   // 3 42 65
}
```

## In real use

Where this feature carries real work, validated by `check_doc_drift.sh examples`:

Example: @TIM-002 — `"next tuesday" as DateTime` cannot fail, so it answers the epoch: a real instant that compares, formats and stores like any other

title: `vector<T>` — append, index, slice, comprehensions, aggregates, map/filter/reduce
body:
## What it is

A growable list of values of one type. Add to it with `+=`, read an item by position (`v[0]`), ask its length with `len(v)`, and build a new list from an existing one with a comprehension.

## How it aids you

It is the go-to container for "a bunch of things" — a list you grow as you go and transform in a single line, without keeping track of the size yourself.

## Example

```loft
fn main() {
    v: vector<integer> = [1, 2, 3];
    v += [4];                              // grow
    doubled = [for x in v { x * 2 }];      // build a new list from it
    println("first={v[0]} len={len(v)} doubled_first={doubled[0]}");
    // first=1 len=4 doubled_first=2
}
```

body:
## What it is

A named type that groups related values together as fields. Create one by naming its fields; read a field with a dot. Fields can carry modifiers, and they are not all the same kind of thing — one is checked by the compiler, one at run time, and one only decides how the value is stored:

- **`const`** — set once at construction; assigning it afterwards is a compile error.
- **`= default`** — the value to use when a literal leaves the field out. Without one, an omitted field takes its type's zero.
- **`computed(expr)`** — worked out on every access and never stored, with `$` naming the record: `area: float computed(3.14159 * $.radius * $.radius)` follows `radius` for free and costs no space.
- **`assert(...)`** — a rule loft enforces at RUN time: a write that breaks it stops the program with `field constraint failed on <Type>.<field>`.
- **`limit(lo, hi)`** — chooses how the integer is STORED (`u8` *is* `integer limit(0, 255)`), and is not enforced. A value outside the range is neither refused nor reported — today it is dropped, wrapped, or stored as `lo`, depending on the width (loft#984). Write `assert(...)` when you want the range checked, or use a narrow type (`u8`, `i16`) when you want the compiler to demand a checked cast at every write.
- **`not null`** — deprecated and does nothing; a type is non-null by default and loft says so when it sees one.

## How it aids you

Instead of juggling several loose variables that belong together, you keep them in one named thing — easier to pass around, and the field names say what each value means. `const`, `assert(...)` and `computed(...)` put the rule next to the data it governs, so an identifier that must never change, a value that must stay in range, or a number derived from the others says so where it is declared rather than in every function that touches it.

## Example

```loft
struct Account {
    const id: integer,
    name: text = "unnamed",
    balance: integer limit(0, 1000000),
}

fn main() {
    a = Account { id: 7, balance: 250 };
    println("{a.id} {a.name} {a.balance}");   // 7 unnamed 250
    a.balance = 300;                          // an ordinary field changes
    println("balance {a.balance}");           // balance 300
}
```

`name` was omitted at construction, so it took its default. Assigning `a.id` is a compile error — a `const` field is fixed once the record exists.

## In real use

Where this feature carries real work, validated by `check_doc_drift.sh examples`:

Example: @IMG-004 — a colour channel declared `limit(0, 255)`: doubling a bright one stores 0, so brightening turns the brightest pixels black
Example: @FTR-006 — which modifiers constrain, and which only choose the storage

body:
## What it is

A function is a named piece of logic you can run whenever you like. You list what it takes in, say what it gives back, and write the steps once — then call it by name as often as you want. Mark a function `pub` to share it so other files can use it too — `pub` is what crosses a file boundary even inside one package, so an unmarked helper stays private to the file that declares it.

A declared result has to arrive on **every** path: a route that falls off the end of a `-> T` function is a compile error (*"expected text, got void on return from block"*), not a zero value slipped in for you.

The other direction is not checked. **A result you ignore is discarded in silence** — `edit(doc);` as a statement compiles, runs, allocates whatever it allocated, and throws the answer away. For an API of pure functions that is the whole failure mode, so bind the result.

## How it aids you

Write a calculation or task in one place and reuse it everywhere, instead of copying the same lines around. Each function has a clear name and a clear result, so your program reads as a list of intentions rather than a wall of detail — and `pub` lets you build a toolbox that other parts of your code can call.

loft reads the shape of the function back to you as you write it: code after a `return` is reported (`unreachable-code`), and a function whose nesting has grown past what a reader can hold is too (`function-complexity` names the deepest line, where a split pays).

## Example

```loft
pub fn square(n: integer) -> integer {
    n * n
}
fn greet(name: text) -> text {
    "Hello, {name}"
}
fn main() {
    println(greet("world"));               // Hello, world
    println("square(6) = {square(6)}");    // square(6) = 36
}
```

## In real use

Where this feature carries real work, validated by `check_doc_drift.sh examples`:

Example: @ZTX-001 — an editing engine of pure functions: every call RETURNS a new document and the one passed in is untouched, so a discarded result is an editor where typing does nothing

title: Named arguments + default parameter values
body:
## What it is

Pass a function's arguments by name — `connect(host: "db", port: 5432)` — instead of only in order, and give parameters default values so callers can leave them out.

## How it aids you

Call sites read like their own documentation, and you can set just the one option you care about without listing everything before it. Both spellings of a call take names, so `cfg.render(dry: true)` and `render(cfg, dry: true)` are the same call.

Adding a defaulted parameter later does not break the **calls** people already wrote — but it does break the places that use the function as a **value**. A default is not part of the function's type, so `fn(integer) -> integer` no longer matches once a second parameter arrives, however optional it is, and a fn-ref call must pass it explicitly. Grow the signature of something you have handed out as a value and you are making a breaking change.

## Example

```loft
fn connect(host: text, port: integer = 8080, tls: boolean = true) -> text {
    "{host}:{port} tls={tls}"
}
fn main() {
    println(connect("example.com"));              // example.com:8080 tls=true
    println(connect("example.com", tls: false));  // example.com:8080 tls=false
    println(connect(host: "db", port: 5432));     // db:5432 tls=true
}
```

## What a default may be

A default is an expression, not a constant, and it is evaluated **at the call** — once per call, and
not at all when the caller supplies the argument. It can read a parameter declared before it:

```loft
fn window(rows: integer, height: integer = rows * 10) -> integer { height }
window(4)      // 40 — the default reads `rows`
window(4, 7)   // 7  — the default is not evaluated
```

title: `const` parameters
Method dispatch via `self` / `both`
body:
## What it is

A method is a function that belongs to a value. Its first parameter is named `self`, which stands for the value you call it on, and you run it with a dot: `value.method()`.

## How it aids you

Related actions live together with the data they work on, so you write `circle.area()` instead of passing the circle into a loose function. Your code reads left to right like a sentence, and it is easy to find every action a value knows how to do.

## Example

```loft
struct Circle {
    radius: float
}
fn area(self: Circle) -> float {
    3.14159 * self.radius * self.radius
}
fn main() {
    c = Circle { radius: 2.0 };
    println("area = {c.area()}");    // area = 12.56636
}
```


## `self`, `both`, and what actually separates them

The reference has long said `self` is method-only, `both` is both forms, and a plain first-parameter name is free-only. Measured, that is two behaviours rather than three:

| first parameter | `p.f()` | `f(p)` | as a fn-ref (`map(v, f)`) |
|---|---|---|---|
| `self` | yes | **yes** | no |
| `both` | yes | yes | no |
| a plain name | no — refused, naming the free form | yes | yes |

A free call resolves by receiver type, so `f(p)` reaches a `self` method too. What separates `self` and `both` is registration, and it shows in the one place neither reaches: **a method is not a function VALUE**, so it cannot be passed to `map` / `filter` or to a parameter of function type (loft#1008). Wrap it — `map(v, |q| { q.f() })` — or declare the function with a plain first-parameter name and give up the dot.

## In real use

Where this feature carries real work, validated by `check_doc_drift.sh examples`:

Example: @FTR-042 — a method reached with a dot: `self` as the receiver, a method returning its own type, and one that mutates the receiver

body:
## What it is

A function's name can be used as a value all by itself. Store it in a variable, pass it to another function, or keep it for later — all without the parentheses that would run it right away.

## How it aids you

Choose behaviour while your program is running and pass it around like any other value: pick which action to apply, or hand a function to a helper like `map` to run over your data. Your code gets to decide not just what data to use but which action to take.

A function value goes anywhere a value goes — a local, a vector element, a struct field, an argument — and a lambda that captured something goes there too. Taking a behaviour as a PARAMETER is how a library stays honest about what it does not own: an engine that asks for its measurement function cannot secretly depend on a font, and a kernel that asks for its event handler cannot depend on your game.

## Example

```loft
fn double(x: integer) -> integer {
    x * 2
}
fn main() {
    f = double;
    println("f(21) = {f(21)}");        // f(21) = 42
    doubled = map([1, 2, 3], double);
    println("{doubled}");              // [2,4,6]
}
```

## In real use

Where this feature carries real work, validated by `check_doc_drift.sh examples`:

Example: @ZTX-004 — a text layout engine takes `resolve` and `measure` as function parameters, so identical output on the interpreter, `--native`, wasm and the browser is a consequence of the signature rather than a promise
Example: @EHK-001 — a server kernel takes its event and tick handlers as arguments, so user code supplies meaning while the kernel owns the loop

Repeat a block once for each item in a collection, or for each number in a range.

title: Pattern matching — enum/scalar/tuple, guards, or-patterns, exhaustiveness
body:
## What it is

`match` picks one branch by comparing a value against a list of patterns, and gives back that branch's result. A pattern can be a specific value, a range, several options at once, a guard, or a catch-all. On an enum, every variant has to be covered.

## How it aids you

One clear choice replaces a long chain of `if` / `else if`, and the chosen result drops straight into a variable instead of being set piece by piece across branches.

"Covered" is enforced two ways, and it is worth knowing which one you are getting. For a CLOSED set — an enum — a missing case is a compile error naming it (`match on Dir is not exhaustive — missing: South`). For an OPEN one — `integer`, `text` — there is no such list to check against, so the arms are enforced by the TYPE instead: a match with no `_` compiles, and a value no arm covers answers `null`. Writing `_` is what makes the result non-nullable.

That `null` is reported only where it meets a non-null context — returning the match into a declared `text` warns, binding it to a local does not. So on an open domain, add `_` (or a `null` arm) unless you mean the fall-through to be an absent value.

## Example

```loft
fn grade(score: integer) -> text {
    match score {
        null     => "absent",
        90..=100 => "A",
        80..90   => "B",
        _        => "other"
    }
}
fn main() {
    println(grade(95));  // A
    println(grade(85));  // B
    println(grade(50));  // other
}
```

`..=` includes its end and `..` does not, and the first arm that matches wins — so `90`
is `"A"` because `90..=100` is listed before `80..90`. The `null` arm catches a genuine
absence, such as reading past the end of a vector. Its price is the in-band sentinel:
the most negative integer IS null, so that one value cannot be told from "absent".

Two more pattern forms, neither shown above: several options in one arm
(`1 | 3 | 5 => "odd"`), and a guard that narrows one (`x if x > 10 => "big"`).

## In real use

body:
## What it is

The usual operators, all built in: arithmetic (`+ - * / %` and `**` for powers), comparison (`== \!= < <= > >=`), logic (`and`, `or`, `\!`), and bit operations (`| & ^ << >>`).

## How it aids you

Everything you expect for calculating and comparing is there with familiar spelling and sensible precedence, so expressions read the way you would say them aloud — and one line can do real work.

There is one place where it does not, and loft warns about it: a leading `-` is the SIGN of what follows, so it binds tighter than `**`. `-x ** 2` is `(-x) ** 2` — 9 when `x` is 3, where reading it aloud gives -9. The same symbol with a left operand goes the other way (`0 - x ** 2` IS -9), so write `-(x ** 2)` when you mean to negate the power. `warning[unary-minus-binds-tighter]` says so — except when the base is a LITERAL, on the grounds that `-3` reads as one number: `-3 ** 2` is 9 and `-1.5 ** 2.0` is +2.25, both silently.

## Example

```loft
fn main() {
    a: integer = 7;
    b: integer = 2;
    println("{a + b} {a - b} {a * b} {a / b} {a % b} {a ** b}");   // 9 5 14 3 1 49
    println("{a > b} {a == b} {a > 0 and b > 0} {a | b} {a & b}"); // true false true 7 2
}
```

## In real use

Where this feature carries real work, validated by `check_doc_drift.sh examples`:

Example: @FTR-012 — the one operator that does not read the way you say it aloud: `-x ** 2` is `(-x) ** 2`

title: Arithmetic safety — overflow/÷0 → null, nullable peers
body:
## What it is

When an INTEGER calculation cannot give a real answer — a number grows too big to hold, you divide by zero, or you take a remainder by zero — loft produces `null` for that result and keeps running, instead of crashing.

**Floats do not follow that rule.** `1.0 / 0.0` is `+inf` and `1.0e308 * 10.0` overflows to `inf`; both are *present* values, so `?? fallback` does not fire and the infinity flows on through every later sum and comparison. The one float division that answers null is `0.0 / 0.0`, because NaN is what loft uses for a null float — so whether `x / d ?? 0.0` defends anything depends on whether the numerator happened to be zero. For a float, test the divisor; `??` is the guard for the integer case (loft#983 tracks the remaining split between a raw quotient and a guarded one).

## How it aids you

One bad integer calculation no longer takes down the whole program. The trouble spot becomes a `null` you can spot and handle (often with `??` to supply a fallback), the way a spreadsheet shows an error in one cell while the rest of the sheet still works.

For a float the cell is not marked, which is what makes the divisor test worth writing: an infinity looks like a number all the way to the file you save.

## Example

```loft
fn main() {
    big: integer = 9_000_000_000_000_000_000;
    total = big + big;          // overflow -> null, no crash
    println("{total}");         // null
    divisor: integer = 0;
    safe = 100 / divisor ?? -1; // divide by zero -> null -> fallback
    println("{safe}");          // -1
    println("done");            // program keeps running
}
```

## In real use

Where this feature carries real work, validated by `check_doc_drift.sh examples`:

Example: @FTR-005 — the integer contract, and the float shapes `??` cannot reach
Example: @MSH-005 — a library that divides by a length and discharges with `?? 0.0`, and the black frame that follows a degenerate camera

title: Math & trigonometry library
body:
## What it is

A set of ready-made number functions: absolute value, the smaller or larger of two values (`min` / `max`), square root, powers (`pow`), the trigonometry functions (`sin` / `cos` / `tan`) and their inverses (`asin` / `acos` / `atan`), rounding (`floor` / `ceil` / `round`), logarithms (`log(value, base)` and the natural `ln`), and the constant `PI`. Each has a `float` and a `single` form.

`round` goes half away from zero: `round(2.5)` is 3 and `round(-2.5)` is -3.

## How it aids you

Reach for the operation you need by name instead of spelling out the formula by hand — one call for a square root, a power, or an angle — so numeric code stays short and reads the way you would say it out loud.

## Example

```loft
fn main() {
    println("abs: {abs(-7)}");            // abs: 7
    println("min/max: {min(3, 9)} {max(3, 9)}");  // min/max: 3 9
    println("sqrt: {sqrt(144.0)}");       // sqrt: 12
    println("pow: {pow(2.0, 10.0)}");     // pow: 1024
    println("cos(0): {cos(0.0)}");        // cos(0): 1
    println("pi: {PI}");                  // pi: 3.141592653589793
}
```

## Six of them can answer null

A domain has holes, and loft spells a hole as null rather than a crash or a NaN you have to test for — NaN IS the null float. So **`sqrt`, `pow`, `log`, `ln`, `asin` and `acos` are declared `float?`** while `abs`, `sin`, `cos`, `tan`, `atan`, `floor`, `ceil`, `round`, `min` and `max` are total and answer a plain `float`.

An INFINITY is not a hole, and that is the pair to get right: `log(0.0, base)` is negative infinity and `1.0 / 0.0` is positive infinity, so `??` never fires on either, while `sqrt(-1.0)` and `asin(2.0)` are null and it does.

Nothing above shows this, because every argument in it is a LITERAL and a literal folds — `sqrt(144.0)` is statically 12.0, so it binds to a plain `float`. The same call on a variable does not:

```loft
x: float = sqrt(144.0);          // fine — folded to a non-null constant
v = 144.0;
x: float = sqrt(v);              // refused: cannot change type from float to float?
y = sqrt(v);                     // fine — y is `float?`
z: float = sqrt(v) ?? 0.0;       // fine — discharged
```

Passing one into a non-null parameter compiles and warns, and the value really does arrive null: *"a nullable `float?` is stored into parameter 1 of `f` of the non-null type `float` — it becomes null there"*.

title: File & directory I/O (+ durable-store binding)

## What it is

Read and write files on disk. Open a path with `file(...)`, `write(...)` text into it, read it back with `content()`, check whether a path `exists(...)`, and remove it with `delete(...)`. You can also list what is in a folder with `list_dir(...)`.

## How it aids you

Save results and load them back on the next run — settings, saved games, reports — with plain calls that take a path and hand you the contents, so your program remembers things between runs instead of starting from scratch every time.

## Example

```loft
fn main() {
    note = file("greeting.txt");
    note.write("hello from loft");
    reloaded = file("greeting.txt");
    println("read back: {reloaded.content()}");   // read back: hello from loft
    println("exists: {exists("greeting.txt")}");  // exists: true
    delete("greeting.txt");
    println("exists after delete: {exists("greeting.txt")}");  // exists after delete: false
}
```

title: Random numbers (rand_seed / rand / rand_indices)
body:
## What it is

Reproducible pseudo-random numbers. `rand(lo, hi)` gives a uniformly distributed integer in `[lo, hi]` inclusive; `rand_seed(seed)` fixes the sequence; `rand_indices(n)` gives `0 … n-1` in a random order.

They live in the **`random` package**, not the always-loaded stdlib, so a program says `use random;` first. loft names the package for you when the call does not resolve.

## How it aids you

A seeded generator makes a random program *repeatable*, which is what makes it testable: seed it and the same run produces the same answer every time, so a shuffle or a sample can be asserted against a fixed expectation instead of a range. The generator is PCG64 and starts from a fixed default, so a program that never calls `rand_seed` is still deterministic — reproducibility is the default rather than something you opt into and forget.

`rand_indices(n)` is the one to reach for when you want *distinct* items. Drawing with `rand` repeatedly samples with replacement, so it can hand you the same index twice; a permutation cannot. Take the first `k` of it and you have `k` distinct items — sampling without replacement, and random iteration order, with no rejection loop.

`rand(lo, hi)` answers null when `lo > hi` or either bound is null, rather than guessing at an empty range.

## Example

```loft
use random;

rand_seed(42);
roll = rand(1, 6);              // somewhere in 1..=6, and the same every run

items = ["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"];
order = rand_indices(len(items));   // e.g. [2, 0, 4, 1, 3] — a permutation

// Three DISTINCT items. Calling `rand` three times could repeat one; taking the
// first three of a permutation cannot.
println("{items[order[0]]} {items[order[1]]} {items[order[2]]}");   // c a e
```

Shown as a fragment rather than a whole program on purpose: this is the only feature whose
example needs a registry package, and a `use` that has to resolve one cannot be run inside the
catalogue's per-example timeout on a cold cache. Every other example is self-contained and is
executed on both backends.

## One rule to know

The sequence is per thread. `rand_seed` seeds the thread-local generator, so seeding on one thread does not make a `par` worker reproducible — seed inside the work if you need that.

body:
## What it is

`sizeof(...)` tells you how many bytes a type or value takes up when it is packed for storage — for a built-in type, one of your own structs, or a variable.

## How it aids you

Know the storage footprint of your data before you write it out — useful when you save records to a file or reason about how much space a large collection will need.

## Example

```loft
struct Point { x: integer, y: integer }

fn main() {
    println("integer: {sizeof(integer)}");  // integer: 8
    println("u8: {sizeof(u8)}");            // u8: 1
    println("u16: {sizeof(u16)}");          // u16: 2
    println("Point: {sizeof(Point)}");      // Point: 16
}
```


## What the numbers are

Measured, identical on both backends: `integer` 8, `float` 8, `single` 4, `character` 4, `boolean` 1, and `text` 4 — a text is a reference into the store, so `sizeof` gives you the reference, not the characters. A plain enum is 1.

A struct is the sum of its fields with no padding between them: `struct S { a: integer, b: boolean }` is **9**, not 16. That is what makes `sizeof` usable for a file layout — the packed size is the stored size.

title: Type aliases (`type X = …`)
Library imports / module system (`use` forms, `pub`)
body:
## What it is

`use` brings names — functions and types — from another `.loft` file or an installed library into your file, so you can call them directly. Put `use` lines at the top of the file.

## How it aids you

Split a program across files and pull in shared code — your own helpers or a published library — without copying it, so each file stays focused and the same code is written once and reused.

## Example

Two files side by side. `greetlib.loft` offers a public function; `main.loft` imports it:

```loft
// greetlib.loft
pub fn greet(name: text) -> text {
    "hello, {name}"
}
```

```loft
// main.loft  — imports greet from greetlib
use greetlib::greet;

fn main() {
    println(greet("loft"));   // hello, loft
}
```

The common forms of `use`:

```loft
use mathlib;                 // bring in every public name
use mathlib::sqrt;           // bring in just one name
use mathlib::(sqrt, pow);    // bring in several (parentheses required)
use mathlib::sqrt as root;   // rename on import
use mathlib as m;            // reach names as m::sqrt
```

## One rule to know

A method spelling wins over an imported free function. loft resolves `f(x, …)` as a method on
`x`'s type before it looks at a `use`d library's free `f`, so a library function whose name and
first argument type match a stdlib method cannot be reached by its bare name — only through the
qualifier (`lib::f`). The compiler warns (`shadowed-by-method`) where that happens.

title: The `loft` CLI — run a program, `--interpret` / `--native`, `--timeout`, `--help`
body:
## What it is

The `loft` command runs a program written in loft. Point it at a source file and it compiles and runs the program in one step. By default it builds a fast native binary; `--interpret` runs the program through the built-in interpreter instead. `--timeout` caps how long a run may take, and `--help` lists everything the command can do.

## How it aids you

One command takes you from a `.loft` file to a running program — there is no separate build or install step to manage. You switch between the quick-starting interpreter and the faster native build with a single flag, and `--timeout` stops a runaway program instead of letting it tie up your terminal.

## Example

```
$ loft hello.loft                 # compile and run (native backend, the default)
Hello, world!

$ loft --interpret hello.loft     # run through the interpreter instead
Hello, world!

$ loft --timeout 60 slow.loft     # hard-kill the run after 60 seconds (0 = no limit)

$ loft --help                     # list every option and subcommand
```

A running loft program cannot invoke a command, so the citation below pins the **artefact** instead — the record this tool emits or reads, captured verbatim from a real run, so that a change to the shape a client depends on breaks a test rather than a client. That the command itself runs is guarded by the binary's own Rust suite.

You can try an expression, check what a function returns, or shape a struct without writing a whole program first. `loft introspect prog.loft` shows you how loft sees your program: the bytecode the interpreter runs, the Rust source the native backend generates, the stack-slot layout, and the resolved types. It turns "what is the compiler actually doing with my code?" into something you can read. $ loft introspect --show-rust prog.loft       # just the generated Rust

A built-in source formatter. `loft --format file.loft` rewrites the file in canonical loft style in place; `loft --format-check file.loft` leaves the file alone and just exits non-zero if it is not already formatted. `loft --format -` reads from standard input and writes the result to standard output.

## What it is

The native backend. `loft --native prog.loft` translates your program to Rust and compiles it with `rustc` into a real machine-code binary, then runs it. You get compiled-language speed from the same source you were interpreting, with no rewrite and no separate toolchain to wire up. Reach for `--native-release` when you want the fastest possible run, and use `--native-emit` when you want to see or reuse the Rust that loft produced.

$ loft --native-release prog.loft  # optimised build (rustc -O), for benchmarking

title: Browser / WASM target (`--html` / `--native-wasm`)
body:
## What it is

The browser target. `loft --html prog.loft` compiles your program to WebAssembly and bundles it into a single self-contained HTML file you can open in any browser. `loft --native-wasm prog.loft` emits just the `.wasm` module when you want to embed it yourself.

## How it aids you

The same loft program that runs on your machine can run on a web page, with nothing to install for whoever opens it — one HTML file is the whole deliverable. It is the simplest way to share a demo, a tool, or a game that people can try with a single click.

## Example

```
$ loft --html game.loft            # write a self-contained game.html
$ # open game.html in a browser — no server or install needed

$ loft --native-wasm game.loft     # emit just game.wasm to embed yourself
```

## What a page can carry

The single file is not limited to code. Three declarations in `loft.toml` put content on
the page, and each has a native counterpart so the same source runs both ways:

* `[[font]]` — the page draws with the font you name rather than a fallback. Declare a
  family the browser already has (nothing is downloaded), a `url` to your own server, or
  a provider `stylesheet`; `--html` emits the `@font-face` or `<link>` and awaits
  `document.fonts.load` before the program starts, so the first frame is not drawn in the
  wrong font.
* `[[embed]]` — a file seeded into the page's own filesystem, which is how a game carries
  an asset pack and reads it with one `store_load` call on the desktop and in the browser
  alike. For a pack too large to embed, the same store is read over HTTP range from any
  static file host — see @F93.
* **Audio** — a browser page loads, plays, loops, pans and seeks sampled sound, the way a
  desktop build does.

title: Package management (`loft install`, `loft.toml`, lockfile)
body:
## What it is

loft's package manager. `loft install <name>` downloads a library from the registry and installs it for use; a `loft.toml` file records the packages your project depends on, and `loft.lock` pins each one to an exact version so builds stay reproducible. `loft new <name>` scaffolds a fresh library, and `loft update` refreshes the pinned versions. A single-file script belongs to no project, so it gets the same pin from `loft pin <script.loft>`, written beside it as `<script>.loft.lock`.

## How it aids you

You reuse other people's libraries instead of reinventing them, and the lockfile means the versions you tested are the versions everyone else — and your CI — gets. Declaring dependencies in `loft.toml` keeps a project's requirements in one place that travels with the code.

**The two files do different jobs, and only one of them is the pin.** `loft.toml` records a CONSTRAINT (`random = "0.1.0"`); `loft.lock` records the RESOLUTION, and the lock is what resolution reads. Each `[[package]]` block carries five fields — `name`, `version`, `url`, `sha256`, `source` — so what travels between machines is an artifact rather than a label. The SHA-256 is what makes reproducibility a claim about bytes.

**A declared dependency is not yet a pinned one.** Until `loft install` resolves the constraint into `loft.lock`, the project carries no answer of its own and the resolver falls back to what the box can offer. `advice[undeclared-dependency]` reports the sharper form of the same gap — a `use` that resolved a registry package the manifest never declares at all, so nothing distinguishes *"we depend on this"* from *"this happens to be installed here"*, and the negative gate *drop the dependency and the tests must stop compiling* cannot be written.

**What no field pins is loft itself.** A perfect pin and a broken build are compatible states: a project pinning a release built against an older loft resolves exactly the release it asked for, and can still fail on a rule loft has added since. `[package] contract` is the field that warns about that (`warning[package-contract-drifted]`) and it is optional, so a package released before it says nothing at all.

## Example

```
$ loft new mytool                  # scaffold loft.toml + src/ + tests/
$ loft install markdown            # fetch a library from the registry, and record it
$ loft install markdown@1.2.0      # or pin a specific version
$ loft install                     # resolve every dependency the manifest declares
$ loft update                      # refresh the lockfile to the latest allowed versions
$ loft pin script.loft             # pin the libraries a single-file script uses
```

title: Stack traces (stack_trace)
Test runner (fn test_*, loft --tests / loft test)
body:
## What it is

loft finds and runs your tests for you: any function named `test_*` is a test. `loft --tests <file>` (or `loft test` in a package) discovers them, runs each, and reports which passed. An `assert(...)` that fails marks the test failed.

## How it aids you

There is no test framework to install and no runner to wire up — name a function `test_something`, put `assert`s in it, and it runs. Tests sit right next to the code they check.

## Example

```
// mymath.loft
fn add(a: integer, b: integer) -> integer { a + b }

fn test_add()  { assert(add(2, 3) == 5); }
fn test_zero() { assert(add(0, 0) == 0); }
```

Run them with `loft --tests mymath.loft` — every `test_*` runs and its pass/fail is reported.


## What the runner actually picks up

Two cases, and which one you are in is decided by the file:

**The file names at least one `test_*`.** Then those are the whole set. A zero-parameter
helper beside them is a helper again, and so is a near-miss name — `testify`, or a function
called exactly `test`, is not a `test_*`:

```loft
fn setup() { println("SETUP RAN"); }
fn test_one() { assert(1 == 1, "ok"); }
```

```
$ loft --tests repro.loft
  ok    repro.loft  (1 fn: test_one)
```

Nothing reports the near-miss: the run says `ok`, having never called it. (A camel-case
`testDouble` cannot catch you out — loft refuses that as a function name.)

**The file names none.** Then arity decides, which is the only reason `--tests` can be
pointed at a plain program at all: every zero-parameter function runs, `main` included,
value-returning ones too, each counted in the total. A function that takes a parameter —
even an unused one — is the only thing skipped, and so today's way to say "not a test"
(loft#1010).

Exit codes are right either way: 1 when something fails, 0 when nothing does.

The count on the per-file line is the cheapest reading of the rule, and a loft file cannot
check it about itself; `tests/test_discovery_rule.rs` asserts both cases and that the
`--native` entry-point generator runs the same set.

## In real use

Where this feature carries real work, validated by `check_doc_drift.sh examples`:

Example: @FTR-056 — which functions a run picks up: the `test_*` a file names are the whole set, and where a file names none, a parameter is what opts out

The **debug adapter** (DAP) lets you set breakpoints, step, inspect locals and evaluate

debugger: every capability already exists behind the `--rpc` debug engine (@I83), and this
layer adds only the DAP framing and handshake, holding the debuggee in-process.

Underneath the language server, the parser records what each identifier occurrence
actually resolves to as it parses. That index is what lets "what is this symbol?" and
"where else is THIS binding used?" be answered precisely rather than by matching names as

title: Direct C binding — `#c "symbol" "signature"`, no rustc and no glue crate
body:
## What it is

Declare a C function in loft and call it. You write the symbol name and its C signature on the declaration — `fn c_abs(v: integer) -> integer;   #c "abs" "int(int)"` — and that is the whole binding: no wrapper crate, no build script, no code generator, and no Rust toolchain.

The signature string is what loft uses to marshal the call, so the declaration is the only place the C types are written down. A `[c] libs` entry in `loft.toml` names a library to load; `[c] optional-libs` marks one that may be absent, and `c_library_available("libfoo.so.1")` asks before calling. A `[c] shim` entry names ANSI-C sources loft compiles for you with `cc`, for the shapes a direct call cannot express — the list is in the third boundary below.

## How it aids you

Use the C library that already exists instead of waiting for someone to port it. Because the declaration carries the signature, there is nothing to keep in sync — no second file that can drift from the first — and because C already has a stable ABI and a name-addressable symbol table, loft needs no generated adapter the way a Rust binding does. Installing a `#c` library needs a C library on the machine and nothing else.

A loft `text` arrives as `const char*` — a pointer to its UTF-8 **bytes**. So a C function that counts them agrees with `size()`, never with `len()`, which counts characters; the two answers come apart the moment the text stops being ASCII.

**Three boundaries to know.**

**The register class**, which is the one you meet first. Every argument and the return travel through fixed integer-class trampolines, so what a binding can express is decided by the register class of each slot — not by its width, and not by how exotic the function is. Integers and pointers (and therefore a `text`) cross directly. A 64-bit **float argument** does not: it travels in an SSE register the caller never writes, so `#c "fabs" "double(double)"` is refused. The two ends of one signature part company here — a float **return** crosses fine, which is why `#c "atof" "double(const char*)"` binds and `double(double)` does not. Also refused: a nullable value (C has no null model), a struct by value, varargs, an out-parameter, and a `vector` whose element width does not match the C pointee. Each has an ANSI-C shim as its cure, which is what `[c] shim` is for. A binding covers **0..=32** C arguments; the 33rd is `error[c-binding-not-interpretable]`. Unlike the wasm boundary below, this refusal is not call-site-conditional — the declaration alone fails the build, with the function never called.

**wasm.** A wasm module cannot open a shared library, so `--native-wasm` and `--html` refuse a `#c` call in one message naming the function, the symbol, the package and the target — here a declaration *is* still portable and only a *call* is refused, so a library may carry `#c` bindings and still build for wasm as long as the wasm program does not reach one.

**The sandbox.** Under `--sandbox` a `#c` binding is gated by `native_ffi`, never by a `#cap` grant: a capability says what data a script may touch, and a C call runs machine code loft cannot inspect.

## Example

```loft
fn c_abs(v: integer) -> integer;      #c "abs" "int(int)"
fn c_strlen(s: text) -> integer;      #c "strlen" "size_t(const char*)"
fn c_atof(s: text) -> float;          #c "atof" "double(const char*)"

fn main() {
    println("abs: {c_abs(-7)}");           // abs: 7
    println("strlen: {c_strlen("loft")}"); // strlen: 4
    // A float RETURN crosses; a float ARGUMENT would need an ANSI-C shim.
    println("atof: {c_atof("2.5")}");      // atof: 2.5
}
```

title: Paged & remote store loading — read part of a dataset over HTTP range
Type-directed interpolation — a type receives the literal/hole boundary
Value structs (`value struct`) — copy semantics, stored inline
body:
## What it is

A `value struct` is a struct with **copy semantics**. Reading one out of a field or a vector element gives you an independent copy, so changing that copy never writes back through the source. Stored inline with no per-element allocation, a `vector<value struct>` costs the same as the raw scalar layout.

## How it aids you

Small geometric things — a point, a colour, a size — behave the way you expect a number to behave when you **bind** one: `q = p.points[0]` is your own copy, and writing it cannot reach back into `p`. You get that without paying for a heap allocation per element, so a vector of a million points is a flat block of memory rather than a million separate records.

The copy is the bind, not the call. **Handing a value struct to a function passes the place itself** — `poke(p.points[0])`, or any `self` method — so the callee's field write lands in your record. Bind it first when you mean to hand over a copy.

## Example

```loft
value struct Point { x: integer, y: integer }

struct Path { points: vector<Point> }

fn main() {
    p = Path { points: [Point { x: 1, y: 2 }, Point { x: 3, y: 4 }] };
    q = p.points[0];    // q is an independent COPY of element 0
    q.x = 99;           // writing it cannot reach back into p
    println("copy {q.x}, source {p.points[0].x}");   // copy 99, source 1
}
```

A value struct is never null: `value struct?` is a compile error, and every one must be initialised. So a fallible constructor cannot answer one *and* signal failure — keep the failure at the underlying type (a `parse` that answers null) and wrap the checked value afterwards.

title: `x?` default-fallback operator — discharge a nullable to its type default
body:
## What it is

Postfix `x?` turns a nullable value into a plain one by falling back to that type's **default** when it is null — `0` for a number, `""` for text, `false` for a boolean.

## How it aids you

When any sensible default will do, `x?` says so in one character, instead of spelling out `?? 0` at every use. It binds tightest, so `a.b?` reads the field then discharges it.

## Example

```loft
struct Config { retries: integer?, name: text? }

fn main() {
    c = Config { retries: null, name: null };
    println("retries {c.retries?}");   // retries 0
    println("name [{c.name?}]");       // name []
}
```

A record has a default even when it declares none for its fields: each field takes its own type's zero, so a missing `Point` discharges to `Point { x: 0, y: 0 }` — nested records, vectors and text included. A declared `= default` wins over that zero, which is the reason to write one.

What has no default is a FIELD whose type has none, and that is a plain `enum` with no variant chosen. loft refuses `?` there and names the field: *"record `WithEnum` has no default: field `c: Colour` is an enum with no explicit choice — add `c: Colour = <variant>`, or make it `Colour?`"*.

Use `??` when you want a *specific* fallback instead of the type's default.

title: `len` vs `size` — logical count vs bytes occupied
body:
## What it is

`len(x)` is a **logical count** and `size(x)` is the **bytes occupied**. For text that is the distinction that matters: `len` counts characters, `size` counts bytes.

## How it aids you

Multi-byte text stops being a trap. When you ask how long a word is, you get characters — what a reader means by length. When you are sizing a buffer or a file record, you ask for `size` and get bytes. Reaching for `len` where bytes were meant is the classic way text handling silently truncates.

## Example

```loft
fn main() {
    s = "café";
    println("len {len(s)} size {size(s)}");   // len 4 size 5
}
```

`é` is one character and two bytes, so the two answers differ — which is the point.

body:
## What it is

Match patterns extend to **sequences**: a `match` arm can describe a run of elements — one after another, alternatives, optional parts, repetition — and capture pieces of it while it goes.

## How it aids you

Recognising a shape in a list stops being a hand-written loop with an index and a pile of `if`s. You write the shape you are looking for and name the parts you want out of it, which is the same thing a grammar does — so small parsers, tokenisers and protocol readers read like their specification.

## Example

```loft
enum Tok { Kw { k: integer }, Num { n: integer } }

fn main() {
    v: vector<Tok> = [Kw { k: 1 }, Num { n: 5 }];
    total = match v {
        [Kw { k }, Num { n }] => k + n,
        _ => -1,
    };
    println("matched {total}");   // matched 6
}
```

Sequence patterns compose: `(a)?` makes a part optional, `a | b` alternates, `..rest` binds the tail, and a failed branch reverts the cursor so the next arm sees the original position.

title: Dead-code lint — a local never read, and a write whose value is lost
body:
## What it is

A lint that points out a local you never read, and a write whose value nothing ever uses — including the case where you copied a collection, changed the copy, and the change went nowhere.

## How it aids you

The dangerous half is the silent one. `d = self.data; d[i] = x` binds a **copy**, so the write is lost and the program keeps running with the original data. A published drawing library shipped every one of its primitives as a no-op through exactly that shape. The lint names the line instead of leaving you to notice the missing output — and it names the function that made the copy, not the call site, which is where a reader would otherwise start looking.

## Example

```
advice: `d` is written but never read — the write is lost
  --> canvas.loft:12:5
   |
12 |     d[i] = colour;
   |     ^
```

Both halves are **warnings**, not advice — ignoring one produces a wrong answer, which is loft's rule for the gating tier — so a build run with `LOFT_DENY_WARNINGS=1` stops on them. `LOFT_NO_DEAD_STORES=1` turns the lost-write half off.

The real message names the mechanism:

```
warning[lost-write]: 'd' is mutated but its value is never read — the write is LOST.
  A whole-value bind (`d = …`) COPIES the heap value (C86), so the mutation lands in
  the copy, not the source.
```

Two limits worth knowing. Guarding with `if i < len(d)` does **not** count as reading `d` — a length cannot witness an element write. And the lost-write half runs on the program path only: under `loft test` it is silent today (loft#985), which is exactly where a library's CI would look.

## In real use

title: The build phase — `loft build`, declared targets, zero-config defaults
body:
## What it is

`loft build` builds a project's **targets** — a target being a named shape (native binary, browser page, WASI module) with the toolchain it needs. The built-in targets are implicit, so a project with no configuration at all still builds.

## How it aids you

Producing every artefact your project ships becomes one command rather than a remembered list of flags per platform. Adding a target is a few lines of manifest instead of a script, and the runtime each shape links is built and kept separate for you.

## Example

```bash
loft build              # build the default targets (native, if unset)
loft build html wasi    # build the named targets
loft build path.loft    # a .loft positional overrides the entry point
```

A `[build]` section overrides the built-ins or adds targets of your own:

```toml
[build]
default-targets = ["native", "html"]

[build.target.html]
features = ["random", "png"]
```


A running loft program cannot invoke a command, so the citation below pins the **artefact** instead — the record this tool emits or reads, captured verbatim from a real run, so that a change to the shape a client depends on breaks a test rather than a client. That the command itself runs is guarded by the binary's own Rust suite.

title: `deliver` / `expose` — hand a loft value to JavaScript with no copy
body:
## What it is

`deliver` hands a whole loft value — a record, a vector, nested to any depth — to JavaScript in the browser with **no serialisation and no copy**. JavaScript reads it straight out of WebAssembly memory, guided by a layout description loft sends along with it. `expose` keeps a value readable across frames; `release` lets it go.

## How it aids you

The usual cost of getting data out of WebAssembly is converting it to JSON and parsing it on the other side, which is both slow and a second description of your types to keep in sync. This removes both: a scalar vector arrives as a typed-array view over the same bytes, so handing over a million numbers costs the same as handing over one.

## Example

```js
// In the page: read the value the loft program delivered.
const value = readLoftValue(tag);
console.log(value.points.length);   // a typed-array view, not a copy
```

Keyed collections (hash, index, sorted, spatial) are flattened to arrays at delivery, so the reader only ever sees scalars, text, records, vectors and enums.

Copy and move semantics — when two names share data, and when they do not
body:
## What it is

Three rules decide whether two names share data or hold separate data.

**Naming a whole value copies it.** `b = a` gives `b` its own copy. Writing `b` does not
change `a`.

**Reading an element out of a container gives you a view of it.** `e = v[0]` does not copy.
`e` is another name for that element, so writing `e` changes the element inside `v`.

**Handing a value to a function follows the type, not the bind rule.** A scalar parameter is a
copy. A struct, value struct or collection parameter names the caller's own value, so a field
or element write inside the callee lands in the caller's record; only replacing the whole
binding needs `&` (@F21). A closure capture splits the same way: a scalar is snapshotted, a
store-backed value is shared in both directions (@F22).

A copy costs time and memory, so loft skips it when it safely can:

- **If you never use the source again, loft transfers the value instead of copying it.** This
  is called a *move*. `h = Holder { v: src }` copies when `src` is used later, and moves when
  it is not.
- **Building the value where it belongs avoids the copy entirely** — `h = Holder { v: [1, 2,
  3] }` never makes a second copy, because there was never a first one.

When loft makes a copy that it could have avoided, it tells you, and it names the variable
that kept the value alive.

A view can stop being a view. A view is another name for a PLACE inside a container, so it
lasts only as long as that place does. Three things end it, and in each case loft gives the
binding its own copy — taken where you wrote it, so it holds the value you bound — and says so,
because writes through it no longer reach the container:

- **Removing** from the container. The positions of the remaining elements change, so the view
  can no longer follow its element.
- **Writing a key field** through the view, on a keyed collection. The element would end up
  reachable by no key at all.
- **Reassigning the container itself** (`bx = Thing { … }`). The view names a place inside
  `bx`, and giving `bx` a new value leaves nothing for it to point at.

To keep writing through after any of these, read the view again.

Changing what is IN the place is not the same as ending the place: `o.inner = Box { n: 9 }`
writes into the place `o.inner` already occupies, so a view of it sees the new value and still
writes through.

## How it aids you

You can tell, by reading your own code, whether two names share data — without knowing
anything about the compiler. A whole-value name is separate; an element read is shared.

You are never charged for a copy silently. When one happens that did not have to, loft names
it and names the variable responsible, so you can decide whether to restructure or leave it.
That turns performance work into something you can see rather than guess at.

## Example

```loft
struct Box { n: integer }
struct Holder { b: Box, tag: integer }

fn main() {
    a = Box { n: 1 };
    b = a;              // whole-value bind — `b` is an independent copy
    b.n = 2;
    println("{a.n} {b.n}");        // 1 2  — writing `b` left `a` alone

    v = [Box { n: 10 }];
    e = v[0];           // element read — `e` is a view of the element
    e.n = 20;
    println("{v[0].n}");           // 20   — writing `e` reached the vector

    h = Holder { b: Box { n: 30 }, tag: 1 };
    w = h.b;            // a view into `h`
    h = Holder { b: Box { n: 40 }, tag: 2 };   // `h` reassigned — `w`'s place is gone
    println("{w.n} {h.b.n}");      // 30 40 — `w` kept the value it was bound to
}
```

`#superseded` — steer callers to a newer form without breaking the old one
body:
## What it is

Sometimes a better way to write something arrives after the old way has already shipped.
loft never answers that by removing the old way — a program that works keeps working. So
instead it gives you a way to *point at* the newer form.

`#superseded "Y"` on a function says: this is superseded by `Y`. Anyone calling it sees a
note naming `Y`, and the old form keeps working exactly as before, for good. It is a
signpost, not a removal, and there is no later version in which it becomes one.

Two rules keep the signpost honest, and loft checks both every time it compiles:

- **The successor has to exist.** `#superseded "no_such_thing"` is a compile error
  (*"the steer would ship dangling"*), so a signpost can never point at nothing — when the
  file is built as a program. Under `loft test` that check does not run today (loft#985),
  which is worth knowing because a library's CI is a test run.
- **The old form has to call the new one.** The superseded function becomes a thin shim
  over its successor rather than a second implementation of the same idea. If its body
  never calls the successor, loft says so — because two separate implementations drift
  apart, and then the note is sending readers somewhere that behaves differently.

The note reaches only the person who can act on it. It appears when the call is in the code
you are compiling, and stays quiet when the call is inside a library you merely depend on —
being told to modernise someone else's code is noise you cannot do anything about.

## How it aids you

You can improve a library's shape without splitting its users into those who upgraded and
those who did not. Everyone's existing code goes on working; the people writing *new* code
learn the better form at the moment they would otherwise have copied the old one.

And you learn about the improvement from your own compiler, at the call you actually wrote,
rather than from a changelog you had to think to read.

For the reader of a codebase the value is the reverse: a name marked this way tells you it
is settled history, not a live choice you are expected to weigh against its successor.

## Example

```loft
// The successor — the form to use now.
fn scaled(v: integer, by: integer) -> integer { v * by }

// The old form. It keeps working, and its body is a shim over the successor.
fn doubled(v: integer) -> integer { scaled(v, 2) }  #superseded "scaled"

fn main() {
    println("{doubled(21)}");    // 42 — the old form still works, unchanged
    println("{scaled(21, 2)}");  // 42 — and the successor gives the same answer
}
```

Compiling this points at the call on the first line of `main`:

```
advice: `doubled` is superseded — use `scaled` (the old form keeps working)
```

Set `LOFT_NO_STEER` to turn the note off.

## In real use

title: Diagnostic suggestions — what to write instead, checked by running it
body:
## What it is

A diagnostic tells you something is wrong. loft also tells you **what to write instead**,
and can check that advice by trying it.

Every warning and every advice loft raises carries two things: a **code** — a short name in
brackets, like `warning[redundant-coalesce]` — and one or more **fixes**. The code is stable:
the wording of a message may improve, the code will not, so it is what you search for and
what a tool keys on.

```
$ loft prog.loft
warning[redundant-coalesce]: Redundant null coalescing — 'name' is 'not null', default is never used
  --> prog.loft:6:29

note: 1 diagnostic above suggests what to write instead — re-run with `--explain`
```

`--explain` adds the fixes. Each says what to write, what it needs you to confirm, and the
name of the capability it uses — a word you can search for when you want to know more:

```
  fix  delete the `?? <default>`   [null coalescing · @F2]
```

**`loft fix` runs the advice before offering it.** loft holds the analysis that raised the
diagnostic, so it can apply a suggested rewrite to a private copy of your file, analyse it
again, and see whether the problem actually goes away without causing a new one:

```
$ loft fix prog.loft
prog.loft
  prog.loft:3  rename to `compute`  [verified]
```

`loft fix --apply` writes the ones that pass. It only ever writes a fix whose meaning is
settled by your code alone. Anything resting on a judgement — *"if you no longer need that
variable"* — is reported with the condition and left for you, because nobody is there to
agree to it.

Editors get the same three things: the fixes as quick-fixes, the full list under each
problem, and the code as a link to its documentation.

## How it aids you

The second half of a diagnostic is where most of the learning is. Knowing that a `??` is
redundant teaches you nothing; being shown that the field is already non-null, and that the
idiom has a name you can look up, teaches you the language.

You also get to trust it. A suggestion that has been **tried** is different from one that
was pattern-matched: when loft offers to correct a misspelled name, it has already checked
that the corrected program still compiles. So a rename that is the right spelling but the
wrong call is refused rather than written into your file.

And nothing happens behind your back. Fixes are shown, never applied, until you ask.

## Example

```loft
struct Tile { name: text }

fn main() {
    t = Tile { name: "grass" };
    // `t.name` is never null, so this default can never be used — loft says so,
    // and `--explain` shows the fix: delete it.
    shown = t.name ?? "none";
    println("{shown}");
}
```

Run it with `--explain` to see the fix.

## What `loft fix` can act on today

`--explain` prints a fix for every code. **`loft fix` reports only the fixes that carry a
machine edit**, and today those are `unknown-function`, `unknown-field`, `unknown-variable`,
`format-unescaped-brace`, `cast-constant-out-of-range`, `text-parse-may-fail` and
`superseded-call` — six errors and one advice. So `loft fix` on the example above prints
nothing, and neither does it for `not-null-deprecated`, `unreachable-code`,
`upper-case-local`, `never-read` or any other warning. Of the 25 codes marked mechanical it
reaches 5 (loft#1003). Read the rest with `--explain` and apply them yourself.

Where it does reach, it does exactly what it says. This is the whole of it, on one misspelling
whose correction does not fit the call:

```loft
fn compute(a: integer, b: integer) -> integer { a + b }

fn main() { println("{comptue(1)}"); }
```

```
$ loft fix prog.loft
prog.loft
  prog.loft:3  rename to `compute`  [REJECTED (the rewrite introduces an error)]
```

`compute` is the right spelling, and the rename is refused because the rewritten program does
not compile — the call passes one argument where two are required. Give `compute` a single
parameter and the same rename reads `[verified]`; `loft fix --apply` then writes it, and
writes nothing on the rejected one. Without `--apply`, neither file is touched.

`--explain` needs the default `--errors=pretty`: under `--errors=compact` a diagnostic is one
line, and that line carries the code but no fix.

Associated types — an interface names a companion type
body:
## What it is

An interface can name a **companion type** that goes with the implementor, not
only a set of methods. A connection and the cursor it produces are one contract:
`type Rows: Cursor` says "and a row type, which must be a `Cursor`", and a
signature names it as `Self.Rows`.

An implementor writes no `impl` block — satisfaction stays structural — so the
companion is INFERRED from the implementor's own signature: where the interface
wrote `Self.Rows`, the implementor wrote a concrete type, and that is it.

## How it aids you

Without this a cursor has to become state ON the connection, so a connection can
hold only one and the type system cannot say so — a second `select` silently
replaces the first. With it the cursor is its own type, two of them coexist, and
the compiler checks the companion satisfies what the interface promised.

It costs nothing at run time: generics specialise per concrete type, so an
associated type is a compile-time name and the generated code is identical to the
same body written against the concrete types by hand.

## Example

```loft
interface Cursor {
    fn width(self: Self) -> integer
}

interface Source {
    type Rows: Cursor                   // the companion type
    fn open(self: Self) -> Self.Rows    // named in a signature as `Self.<Name>`
}

struct FileRows { w: integer }
struct FileSource { path: text }

fn width(self: FileRows) -> integer { return self.w; }
fn open(self: FileSource) -> FileRows { return FileRows { w: len(self.path) }; }

// The generic holds the companion and calls the bound's methods on it. Two of
// them coexist, which is what a cursor kept ON the connection could never do.
fn total_width<S: Source>(s: S) -> integer {
    a = s.open();
    b = s.open();
    return a.width() + b.width();
}

fn main() {
    println("{total_width(FileSource { path: "abcd" })}");   // 8
}
```

## Rules worth knowing

- **Every position must agree.** The companion is read from the return AND the
  parameters — an implementor whose `open` yields one type while its `feed` takes
  another does not have one companion, and is refused rather than resolved by
  declaration order.
- **The bound is checked per implementor**, and the message names all four
  parties, because three of them are invisible at the call site:
  *"'S1' binds 'Source.Rows' to 'Bad', which does not satisfy the declared bound
  'Cursor': missing width"*.
- **A bound-less `type Held` still binds.** Nothing of the companion's own is
  callable, but the interface that named it can take it back
  (`fn keep(self: Self, h: Self.Held)`).
- The name is a type name and is enforced CamelCase; `Self.<Name>` is spellable
  only inside the declaring interface's body.



## In real use

`OpDrop` — a type runs code when its scope lets it die
body:
## What it is

A type that defines `OpDrop` runs it when a scope that OWNS one lets the value
die — the shape RAII gives a transaction, a file handle or a C resource.

The rule is one sentence:

> A drop runs exactly where the value's own free runs — the same binding, the
> same scope exit, the same early-exit paths — and never anywhere else.

So it inherits every case that is easy to get wrong by hand: an early `return`, a
`break`, a `return` out of a loop that bypasses the loop epilogue, and
reverse-declaration order within a scope.

## How it aids you

Cleanup stops being something a reader has to verify on every path out of a
function. You write the release once, on the type, and the compiler puts it at
each exit — including the ones you would have forgotten.

## Example

```loft
struct Lease {
    id: integer,
}

fn take(id: integer) -> Lease {
    println("take {id}");
    return Lease { id: id };
}

// Runs when a scope that OWNS a Lease lets it die.
fn OpDrop(self: Lease) { println("release {self.id}"); }

fn hold() {
    a = take(1);
    b = take(2);
    println("working");
}

fn main() {
    hold();
    println("done");
}
```

prints

```
take 1
take 2
working
release 2
release 1
done
```

— reverse declaration order, so nothing outlives what it belongs to.

## What it costs, stated up front

**A drop cannot fail.** It runs at a closing brace with no caller left to tell,
and loft has no runtime errors, so `OpDrop` may not return and one that tries is
refused. Anything whose failure MATTERS stays an explicit call:

```loft
tx.commit()      // may fail; you get the answer
// scope end     // best-effort rollback if not committed; you get nothing
```

That asymmetry is the design, not an oversight.

**A drop reaches the world, not its caller's data.** It receives only `self`, and
a struct field COPIES at construction, so a drop cannot write back into a
caller's collection. Its effect is I/O or a resource it owns — which is exactly
the intended use: a `ROLLBACK` on a connection the transaction holds.

That copy is worth stating on its own, because it is the opposite of the rule
everywhere else and a reader who knows the other one will predict wrongly. A
PARAMETER names the caller's record — that is why mutating a struct field
through a plain parameter is visible to the caller and `&` is not needed for it.
A STRUCT LITERAL does not: it copies what it is given. So of these two lines,
one line apart and holding the same vector, the caller sees the first and not
the second:

```loft
fn param(v: vector<integer>)   { v += [7] }                      // caller sees [1,7]
fn infield(v: vector<integer>) { h = H { log: v }; h.log += [8] } // caller still sees [1]
```

The copy boundary is the construction, not the call — which is what leaves a
drop with no route back to its caller's data.

## Other rules worth knowing

- A **returned** value does not drop in the callee; the scope that receives it
  owns it. A **borrowed** argument does not drop in the callee either.
- A binding written inside an `if` block is hoisted to the function scope — that
  is where loft frees it, so that is where it drops. A `for` body IS a scope, so
  a droppable made per iteration drops per iteration.
- A value that was never created never drops.

Example: @FTR-018 — the enumerated cases checked against a hand-computed log, and the struct literal that ends the sharing

title: Library placement — in-process, a worker, or another machine
body:
## What it does

Decides **where** a library's functions run — in this process, in a worker process on this machine, or on a server elsewhere — from one line of the library's own manifest, with the consumer's source unchanged:

```toml
[library]
placement = "inproc" | "process" | "remote"
```

The invariant it holds is that you cannot tell from the program: a call to a library is indistinguishable, in type, effect, ownership/lifetime and error behaviour, from the same call in-process. Where it runs is deployment policy, not source.

A struct or a vector crosses as **itself** — a shared memory-mapped loft store for a worker on this machine, the same store's bytes on a socket for a remote one — rather than being encoded into a second wire vocabulary. That is possible because nothing inside a store is a pointer: a record graph's interior references are plain `u32` record ids, so it is independent of both the address it is mapped at and the store number it is registered under.

What it buys: fault isolation (a crash inside the library ends the call as a loft error instead of taking the program's data with it), and the ability to put a library on the machine that should hold it.

Not everything can be placed, and the rules are the library author's to follow — a public function must not itself be a native, the surface should answer a value rather than a cursor, closures do not cross, and a function returning a borrowed VIEW of something it did not create is refused rather than mis-marshalled. A signature outside what the boundary carries simply runs in-process, byte-identically; nothing becomes a call that fails later.

## Where it lives

`src/lib_placement.rs` (declaration), `src/lib_placement/arena.rs` (the shared store a compound value crosses in), `src/lib_placement/wire.rs` (both transports and both ends), `src/lib_placement/dispatch.rs` (routing a placed library's calls).

Reference: `doc/claude/PLACEMENT.md` (mechanism + authoring rules), `doc/claude/PACKAGES.md` (the declaration).



## In real use

Where this feature carries real work, validated by `check_doc_drift.sh examples`:

Example: @FTR-087 — where a library runs is one manifest line, and the call site cannot tell

title: Git query natives — a repository as a typed library, not a subprocess
body:
## What it does

Lets loft read a git repository through a typed library — `git::log(20) -> vector<Commit>`, `git::changed(base) -> vector<Change>`, `git::tracked_files() -> vector<text>` — instead of through a subprocess primitive. loft deliberately has no `run(cmd, args)`: it hands back bytes and an exit status, and every caller then re-parses text loft already knows how to type.

So the `execve` lives inside one vetted library, and the natives behind it are a **closed query vocabulary**: the caller names a question and loft builds the command. Nothing composes a command line, which is what removes the injection surface by construction rather than by filtering — `git -c core.sshCommand=…` is unreachable, a path always follows `--`, and a ref may not begin with `-`. Reading a repository needs the library's own `git#read` capability, separately from reading files.

Registered for both backends, so a compiled program can ask git too.

## Where it lives

`src/git_query.rs` (the vocabulary and both backends' entry points), registered in `src/native.rs` and `src/codegen_runtime.rs`; the typed loft surface is `lib/git/`.

First consumers: `tools/viewer/refresh.loft` (which replaced 135 lines of bash and the review dashboard's dependency on `jq`) and `tools/indexer/src/scan.loft` (which asks which files the repository carries instead of mirroring `.gitignore` by hand).
