title: Time (now / ticks)
body:
## What it is

Two clocks, for the two questions a program asks about time.

`now()` answers the wall clock: milliseconds since the Unix epoch. It is the one to stamp a
record with, or to compare against a date someone else wrote down.

`ticks()` answers elapsed time: microseconds from an arbitrary start, and it only ever goes
forward. It is the one to measure with — subtract two readings and you have a duration.

They are not interchangeable. A wall clock can jump backwards when the machine syncs its
time, so a duration measured with `now()` can come out negative; `ticks()` cannot do that,
and it has a thousand times the resolution.

## How it aids you

Stamp events with `now()` so they mean the same thing to another program, on another machine,
next year. Time your own code with `ticks()` — a frame, a request, a slow loop — and get an
answer that does not depend on what the clock did while you were measuring.

## Example

```loft
fn main() {
    started = ticks();                      // microseconds, monotonic
    total = 0;
    for i in 0..100000 { total += i; }
    elapsed = ticks() - started;
    println("sum: {total}");                          // sum: 4999950000
    println("measured a duration: {elapsed >= 0}");   // measured a duration: true
    println("clock is set: {now() > 0}");             // clock is set: true
}
```

title: Store locks (#lock)
body:
## What it is

`#lock` is an attribute on any value that lives in a store — a struct, a vector, a keyed
collection. Set it to `true` and every WRITE to that store panics; reads carry on working.
Set it back to `false` and writes are allowed again. A freshly created store starts unlocked.

The guard is on the STORE, not on the name you happened to lock it through, so it fires
wherever the write is written — including inside a function you passed the value to.

## How it aids you

`const` is the compile-time answer to "this must not change", and it is the one to reach for
first: it costs nothing and it catches the mistake before the program runs.

`#lock` is for the case `const` cannot see — a value that is supposed to hold still for part
of its life and is changing anyway, somewhere you have not found yet. Lock it and the program
stops AT the write, with a stack that names it, instead of carrying a wrong value onward to
wherever it finally looks wrong.

## Example

```loft
struct Counter { value: integer }

fn main() {
    c = Counter { value: 5 };
    println("starts unlocked: {!c#lock}");   // starts unlocked: true

    c#lock = true;
    println("locked: {c#lock}");             // locked: true
    println("still readable: {c.value}");    // still readable: 5
    // `c.value = 6` would panic here, and so would a write inside any function
    // handed `c` — the guard travels with the store.

    c#lock = false;                          // lift the guard
    c.value = 6;
    println("written once unlocked: {c.value}");   // written once unlocked: 6
}
```

title: Lexer library (lib/lexer)
body:
## What it is

The `lexer` library breaks text into TOKENS — the smallest pieces that carry meaning:
numbers, names, operators, quoted strings.

You tell it two things about your language and it handles the rest. `set_tokens` lists the
multi-character operators, so `+=` is scanned as one token instead of a `+` and an `=`.
`set_keywords` lists the reserved words, so `let` comes back as itself and never as an
ordinary name.

Then you read tokens in order with typed readers: `int()` takes the next integer or answers
null, `identifier()` takes the next name, `matches(s)` takes the next token only if it is `s`
and says whether it did, `peek()` looks without taking.

⚠ Not to be confused with **@I57 Lexer**, which is loft's OWN lexer — the compiler stage that
reads your `.loft` files. This is a library your program calls to read text of its own.

## How it aids you

Reading a small language — a config format, a rule file, an expression a user typed — is
mostly tokenising, and tokenising by hand is where the fiddly bugs live: two-character
operators split in half, a keyword swallowed as a variable name, positions that drift so the
error points at the wrong line. Hand it the rules and read the pieces back.

It is also half a foundation: pair it with the `parser` library, or layer your own grammar on
top, and the tokeniser is done.

## Example

```loft
use lexer;

fn main() {
    l = lexer::Lexer { };
    l.set_tokens(["+=", "==", "->"]);        // scanned as ONE token each
    l.set_keywords(["let", "in"]);           // reported as themselves, never as names

    l.parse_string("snippet", "let total += 12");
    println("keyword: {l.matches(\"let\")}");   // keyword: true
    println("name: {l.identifier()}");          // name: total
    println("operator: {l.matches(\"+=\")}");   // operator: true
    println("number: {l.int()}");               // number: 12
}
```
